title.scientific: Planetary Formation: From Protoplanetary Disk to Habitable Worlds
title.algorithmic: Planetary Accretion and Differentiation Simulation using Accumulation Models

scientific.concept: Planets form from protoplanetary disks of gas and dust surrounding young stars. The process involves dust particle nucleation, growth by accretion to form planetesimals, gravitational collisions to create protoplanets, and finally internal differentiation and orbital debris clearing.
scientific.analogy: Planetary formation is like making a giant snowball. You start with a small flake (dust grain) that rolls downhill accumulating more snow. As it grows, its gravity attracts more material until it becomes massive enough to 'clear' its neighborhood, leaving only the planet and its moons.
scientific.real_world_example: The Solar System is 4.6 billion years old and shows clear evidence of its formation: the inner rocky planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars) and outer gas giants (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune). The asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter represents material that never accreted due to Jupiter's gravitational perturbations.
key_concepts: Protoplanetary disk: rotating gas and dust cloud around protostar
Planetesimals: 1-10 km bodies formed by dust accretion
Planetary embryo: massive protoplanet dominating its accretion zone
Snow line: distance where ice can exist (affects planetary composition)
Planetary migration: orbital change due to disk interactions
Giant Impact: collision between protoplanets (e.g., Moon formation)
Differentiation: layer separation by density (core, mantle, crust)

algorithmic.algorithm: Gravitational accretion model with N-body numerical integration and inelastic impact accretion

complexity.time: O(n² × t) where n is number of particles and t is time steps; optimizable to O(n log n) with Barnes-Hut
complexity.space: O(n) to store state of all particles

algorithmic.why_this_algorithm: N-body simulation captures the essential gravitational interactions. Impact accretion models how planetesimals grow through collisions. It is the gold standard for planetary formation modeling.

comparison.smoothed_particle: SPH is better for fluids but more expensive
comparison.monte_carlo: Monte Carlo is faster but loses exact orbital dynamics
comparison.statistical: Statistical models are useful for populations but not individuals

visualization_hints.color_mapping: Gradient by mass: blue (small), green (medium), red (large); opacity by density
